label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
# My Van Caught Fire Last Wednesday. Here's Everything I Got Wrong So You Don't Have To.

*October 28, 2:15pm, a driveway in Bedford. I'm writing this four days later because I still haven't really slept. If you came here for the dog content, there's none — it's all cable gauges and fire codes. But I promised Tasha I'd write it up properly, and honestly I need to type this out anyway.*

---

I need to say up front: **I am not an electrician. I don't know code. Everything technical in this post came from Priya at Sackville Marine Electric, and I'm just repeating what she told me while showing me photos.** If any of this scares you, please get someone qualified to look at your van. Don't use my blog post as a substitute for that. I got very lucky. Other people won't.

Here's what happened.

## The setup

- 3000W inverter, 12V
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries, in parallel (so 400Ah total, 12V)
- Built by Coastline Van Fitouts — Darren — spring 2025
- Inverter mounted under the bench seat, batteries in the same compartment under the bench seat
- Cable from the battery bank to the inverter: 4 AWG
- 300A ANL fuse somewhere in that run

I ran a 1800–2000W dryer on high, and sometimes the water heater at the same time. Normal Wednesday. I've done this a hundred times.

## What went wrong

Priya found four things. I'm going to list all four because any one of them on its own worries me, and I had all four at once.

### 1. The cable was too small. Way too small.

A 3000W inverter at 12V pulls roughly **250 amps**. My dryer alone at 1800–2000W is **150–167 amps**. Add the water heater and I'm in the 200–250A range easily.

The cable was 4 AWG. Priya says for 3000W at 12V it should have been **2/0**. She pulled up ampacity tables on her laptop and showed me where 4 AWG sits — roughly in the 110–120 amp range depending on how it's rated and where it's run — and where 2/0 sits, and then she just let me do the subtraction. **I was pushing two to three times what that cable was rated for.**

I want to be clear about something because I think a lot of us get this wrong: the reason a van doesn't catch fire every day is that people don't usually run their hair dryer and water heater simultaneously for four hours while pulling near max output. The inverter was fine. The batteries were fine. The cable was undersized for the load, and it ran hot for over a year and a half, every single time, and I never noticed.

### 2. The lug on the positive end was crimped with pliers.

Not a crimper. Pliers. Or a hammer. Priya's words: "that wasn't a crimp, that was a squeeze."

And here's the part that makes me sick — **there was heat-shrink over it.** So from the outside, looking down at it with the seat flipped up, everything looked *finished*. Tidy. Professional. I never saw it. The heat-shrink was doing the opposite of what it's for: it hid the exact thing that was killing me.

A bad crimp has high resistance. High resistance means heat. That heat travels into the cable jacket, and the jacket melts back, and eventually you have an arc. That's the fire. That's the whole fire. Not the dryer, not the inverter, not the batteries. A hand-squeezed lug slowly cooking itself for eighteen months.

### 3. The fuse was the right idea, mounted in the wrong place.

The 300A ANL was a reasonable size for the job. The problem was **where it was** — about 90 centimetres from the battery positive terminal. Priya said it should have been **within about 18 centimetres** (7 inches) of the battery.

Why does that matter so much? Because the fuse only protects the cable *downstream of itself*. Every centimetre of cable between the battery and the fuse is unprotected. 90cm of unprotected cable means that if anything touched that section — a nail, a chafed edge, a wireloom bracket, a curious dog, anything — you get a dead short with no fuse to catch it. That's an arc flash, not a blown fuse.

I don't fully understand the physics of why 18cm and not 90cm and I asked her three times. Her answer every time: "Because that's where it can protect." Short, correct, and I should have pushed harder when I asked for the build in the first place.

### 4. No smoke detector in the back of the van.

Just the factory one in the cab. Which is on the other side of a bulkhead, behind a closed door, with a dog and a dryer and a water heater and two lithium batteries.

That's not a criticism of the build — I don't know if it was ever specified. But it's a thing I didn't think about, and I should have. There's a smoke detector in my house. There's one in the bedroom. There wasn't one two metres from a battery bank that I run a 2000W heater next to for a living.

## What I actually noticed, in the moment

**2:15pm. Hot plastic smell.** Strong, sweet, chemical. I thought it was the dryer motor overheating because I'd had him on high and I'd been running the water heater. I reached down to check the dryer.

Then I saw smoke coming out of the **bench seat.**

Not flames. Not yet. Just grey smoke pushing up out of the seam of the seat cushion, which is exactly where the batteries live, which is exactly where the lug was.

Here's the thing nobody tells you: your brain does not want to believe your house is on fire. I had a *rational* explanation ready for the smell. It took me maybe two seconds longer than it should have to drop that story.

I killed the battery switch. Got Moose out the side door — he was still damp from the bath, and he was thrilled, tail going, completely unbothered by the smoke, which I will be thinking about for a while.

I used the extinguisher a bit. I still don't know if I needed to. The lug was black. The cable jacket had **melted back about 3 centimetres** from the terminal. There was a scorch mark on the seat frame.

Moose's mom came out with a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook. I want to say something about that, because I was the only person in that driveway who was falling apart, and she didn't try to fix it or ask questions. She just sat there. If you're reading this and your mom brings you coffee — thank you. I mean it.

## The thermal camera comparison

This is the part that made Priya's point better than I ever could.

She pulled up my damage photos. Then she pulled up thermal camera shots of **her own van**, running the same kind of load — same inverter class, same hair dryer, same kind of load on the cables. On the thermal camera, in her van, the cables barely get warm. Just a faint glow at the lug, normal, nothing.

Then she put my photos next to hers.

The difference was **wild**. Not a little different. A completely different outcome from the same equipment and roughly the same load. The only differences were the cable size, the crimp, and the fuse placement. Everything else — the inverter, the batteries, the dryer — was the same.

She said something like: "Your van was working *against itself*. It was just a matter of time and where the weak point happened to be."

I've thought about that every day since. **Tidy is not the same as right.** I trusted the build because it looked clean. Cable runs were neat, everything was labelled, the seat lifted up and you saw a tidy little compartment with tidy little cables. That's what I was paying for. I didn't know to ask about gauge and fuse distance because I didn't know they were choices that got made without me.

## What it has cost me so far

- **Repair quote: $4,200.** Rewire the main runs, new fuse block, class T fuse instead of the ANL. Parts are on order.
- **Minimum three weeks.** Three weeks minimum. Probably longer once they're in and the loom needs re-routing properly.
- **31 appointments cancelled** so far, and I'm still taking bookings for dates I'll have to move.
- **Insurance says maybe.** The adjuster is coming Thursday. "Maybe" is not a word I've ever liked from an insurance company, but I'm holding onto it.
- **Rent is due the 1st.**

I'm 28. This van is my whole income. Not a side thing, not a hobby vehicle — it's the business. Every dollar I have comes out of that van, and right now it sits in a shop with a melted cable under the bench seat.

And Darren hasn't answered my three texts or my email. I'm not going to say more than that. I'm not trying to trash him publicly — I don't know what he's doing, maybe he's travelling, maybe he's in the middle of something. I've read things online about other builders and I don't want to be that person. But I'll say this: **if you build vans for a living and a customer has a fire involving your electrical, not replying to three texts and an email is not great.** That's a fact, and people can decide what to make of it.

What I *will* say is this: there are good builders out there. Ask the questions in the list below before you hand over a deposit, and if you get straight answers, that's a good sign. The issue with mine wasn't obviously bad faith. It was that nobody — including me — asked the questions.

---

# The checklist: what to check on your own van

**Power off. Engine off. Battery switch off. Key out.** Do not do this with the system live. If you're not comfortable, stop and call someone.

I'm going to split this into "what I could check myself" and "what needs a professional." Honestly, the professional list is the important one. But start here.

### Find your numbers and write them down

1. **Find the inverter's wattage.** It's on the label, usually on the side or bottom. Mine is 3000W.
2. **Divide by 12.** 3000 ÷ 12 = **250 amps**. That's your inverter's maximum input current — the most current it will ever try to pull from your batteries.
3. **Add up your biggest possible loads.** My dryer alone is 1800W = 150A. My water heater adds more. If your two biggest loads together exceed your inverter's wattage, that's a problem I had and didn't know about: an overloaded inverter can pull more current than its rating. Ask Priya about this — she explained it to me and I understood maybe 70% of it. **The question to ask is: "What's the worst-case amperage my system can draw, and is my cable rated for that, not for my average load?"**
4. **Find the cable gauge.** It's stamped on the jacket: "4 AWG," "2 AWG," etc. If you can't find it, that's a flag.
5. **Compare.** If the amps exceed the cable's rating, don't drive it like that. Get it looked at.

### Look at the connection

6. **Find every lug and terminal on the battery-to-inverter run.** Flip the seat, pull the covers, look at the raw copper.
7. **Is the heat-shrink on? Is there copper poking out the end?** Fresh copper poking out of a lug means it wasn't crimped right.
8. **Do the lugs look discolored, blackened, or greenish?** Those are signs of heating and corrosion.
9. **Wiggle test.** If a terminal moves or feels loose, that's a bad crimp or a loose bolt. Don't do this with the power on.
10. **Are the terminals clean and tight?** Corroded battery terminals create resistance, which creates heat.
11. **Are the batteries swollen or dented?** If they're lithium, swelling is a serious red flag. Get them checked.

### Look at the fuse

12. **How big is it, and how far is it from the battery?** Mine was 300A, which is fine, but 90cm away. You want it right at the battery — 18cm or so — so the short unprotected length of cable is as short as physically possible.
13. **Is it the right type?** Priya recommended a class T fuse in the repair. I don't know the difference well enough to explain it. Ask.
14. **Is the fuse holder in good shape?** Cracked, melted, loose, or mounted to something that can vibrate — all bad.

### Buy these four things. Today.

15. **A cheap infrared thermometer.** $40 at Canadian Tire. This is the single best piece of advice in this whole post. Point it at your lugs and cables after a long day of heavy loads. If anything is hotter than its neighbours, something's wrong. I wish I'd had one. Priya had one on her thermal camera and it took about ten seconds to show her the difference between her van and mine.
16. **A smoke detector for the back of the van.** I don't care if it's the $30 battery kind from the hardware store. Mine would have given me a minute or two. Get two if you can — one near the battery compartment, one near the cab bulkhead. Test it monthly.
17. **A fire extinguisher you can reach from outside the van.** And know what it's rated for (electrical fires are a specific class — make sure it's rated for it). Know how to use it. Mine was in the cab and I'd never practised with it.
18. **A battery disconnect switch that you can hit without opening anything up.** Mine worked. That's the only reason this story ends with a wet dog and not a catastrophe. Make sure you know where it is *before* you need it, because you will not be thinking clearly.

### Also worth checking

19. **Is your inverter mounted somewhere with airflow?** Lithium batteries and inverters both generate heat, and heat in a closed van compartment is how the heat-shrink-hidden lug became a fire.
20. **Is anything near the batteries that could chafe or pinch a cable?** Cable ties too tight, sharp sheet metal edges, a bracket rubbing in the road.
21. **Is your water heater on the same circuit as your dryer?** Both are big resistive loads and both were running when this happened. I don't know if that's a design flaw or just how it was built, but it's worth asking about.
22. **Are your loads rated for 12V, or are they doing the conversion themselves?** Wet dog, damp towels, water heater, wet floor, and 250 amps of DC in a van. I don't know enough to say whether wet floors matter here. Priya did. I'm asking her to explain that part again and I'll add it to this post when I do.

---

# Questions to ask a builder before you pay a deposit

**Tasha — this part is for you specifically.** You're about to put a deposit down. Do not skip this list. Do not feel bad about asking; any builder worth hiring will respect these questions, and if they get annoyed, that's your answer.

Take this to the meeting. Take notes. If you get any of these in writing, even by email, keep it.

1. **"What size cable is running from the battery bank to the inverter?"** Get the AWG number. Don't accept "it's all marine grade." Get the number.
2. **"What's the inverter's max input current at 12V, and is my cable rated for that?"** They should be able to do this arithmetic on the spot.
3. **"How far is the main fuse from the battery positive terminal?"** If the answer is more than about 18cm, ask why.
4. **"What type of fuse are you using and why?"** They should be able to explain the choice.
5. **"Are all the lugs crimped with a proper crimping tool? Can I see the crimp before you cover it in heat-shrink?"** Actually ask to see it. Heat-shrink hides bad work — that's literally what happened in my van.
6. **"What gauge lugs and terminals are on the battery positive, and are they tinned copper?"**
7. **"Is there a battery disconnect switch, and where is it?"**
8. **"Is there a smoke detector in the back?"** If the answer is no, install one yourself. It's $30.
9. **"What are the maximum simultaneous loads this system is designed for, in watts?"** If your dryer and water heater together are more than the inverter's rating, you need to know before you find out on a Wednesday afternoon.
10. **"Can you walk me through the whole run — battery to inverter to each accessory — and tell me the gauge at each point?"**
11. **"What torque are the battery terminals and lugs supposed to be at?"** And then check they were torqued to it. Loose terminals = heat.
12. **"What's the total cost of the electrical, broken out, and can I see the invoices for the parts?"**
13. **"If something goes wrong with the electrical, what's your warranty, and how do I reach you?"** Ask for a direct number. Mine doesn't answer texts.
14. **"Are you insured for this, and can I see the certificate?"**

And then — this is the one that matters most — **"Can I get a look at a completed van with a similar system before mine goes in?"** And while you're standing in it, look for the things in the checklist above. Flip the seat. Find the fuse. Find the cable stamping.

---

## Where I'm at

The van's in the shop. Parts are on order. Three weeks minimum from the quote, and that's assuming no surprises, which there will be. Insurance adjuster comes Thursday. 31 appointments cancelled so far and I'm rescheduling as fast as I can, but there's a real gap where the money isn't coming in and the rent is still due on the 1st. I'm scared in the way you're scared when the thing your whole life depends on is sitting in someone else's driveway with a melted cable under the seat.

But everyone and every dog is fine. Moose went home damp and happy and has no idea. The client's driveway is fine. Nobody was hurt. I'm going to be able to work again.

Things I'm doing while I'm waiting:

- Getting the adjuster's report so I know exactly what insurance will and won't cover
- Getting Priya back in to walk me through the parts list so I understand what I'm paying $4,200 for, and to check the rest of the van while she's there
- Rebuilding the booking list. If you're in Halifax and you've been waiting on a slot, message me — I'm taking names for a priority list for when I'm back
- Writing the insurance and warranty questions down so I actually ask them and don't get flustered

**I'll update this post when the van's back.** Specifically: what the final repair actually cost, what insurance covers, what the rewire ended up looking like, and — if I can get permission from the other builder — what a properly sized run looks like next to what I had. I want to put photos side by side with Priya's thermal camera shots. The difference is worth seeing.

In the meantime: **go flip your seat. Find your fuse. Find your cable gauge. Write the numbers down.** And if you haven't got an infrared thermometer, that's your Saturday.

And Tasha — **get it in writing before the deposit.** I mean it. You're the one person I can actually do something for here. Ask every question on that list and don't let anyone make you feel difficult about it. My van looked perfect.

— *Me, from my kitchen table, with a lot of coffee, waiting on Thursday*

---

*One more time because it matters: I am not an electrician. Priya at Sackville Marine Electric is. Please get a qualified person to look at your own van. I got lucky and I want you to too.*
